entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Anvari (Awhad ad-Din 'Ali ibn Mohammad Khavarani, c. 1126–1189) was a preeminent Persian poet and polymath of the 12th century, flourishing during the twilight of the Seljuk Sultanate. Hailing from what is now Afghanistan, his literary prowess earned him the esteemed position of court poet under Sultan Sanjar, the last great Seljuk ruler. Anvari stands as a towering figure in classical Persian literature, particularly celebrated as a master of the *qasida* (ode or panegyric), a poetic form he elevated through his intricate language, philosophical depth, and sophisticated wit, profoundly shaping the trajectory of Persian poetic expression. His work not only served as courtly praise but also captured the intellectual and political currents of a dynamic era, making him an invaluable historical and cultural voice.

Born in Abivard (modern Turkmenistan) or Badavard (modern Afghanistan) around 1126, Anvari received a comprehensive education in various sciences, including astronomy, astrology, mathematics, and philosophy, alongside traditional Islamic studies. His early career saw him gain recognition in Balkh before attracting the attention of Sultan Sanjar, whose court in Merv became the epicenter of his poetic output. Anvari’s *Divan* (collected works) comprises thousands of verses, predominantly *qasidas* dedicated to Sanjar and other patrons, but also includes *ghazals*, *rubaiyat*, and *qit'as*. His panegyrics are renowned for their elaborate metaphors, rhetorical flourishes, and subtle allusions to Quranic verses, Hadith, and classical Persian lore. Beyond praise, Anvari also wielded sharp satire and poignant laments, often reflecting on the transient nature of power and the vicissitudes of life following Sanjar’s defeat by the Oghuz Turks in 1153.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Anvari's masterful and innovative approach to the *qasida* profoundly shaped the development of classical Persian poetry, influencing generations of poets and contributing significantly to the Seljuk era's literary canon. His work provides unique insights into 12th-century courtly life and intellectual pursuits.
